6 March
On this day in 1752

The cooperation between Sikhs and Mir Mannu snapped as a result of Kaura Mal’s death

This was evident from action during Abdali’s third invasion. The Sikhs under the patronage of Diwan Kaura Mal, a Khulasa Sikhs, had cooperated with Mir Mannu. henceforth, Mir Mannu as a nominee of Afghans pursued the policy of extirpating Sikhs. If nothing else, their women and children were taken to Nakhas, Lahore, in hundreds, and were subjected to gruesome torture and martyred. In 18 months, he killed about 30,000 Sikhs. The peasantry crushed, because of the Afghan depredations and roving provincial troops in search of the Sikh families, joined the Khalsa fold in large numbers who offered them protection.

6 March brings together four moments of Sikh history, from 1752 to 1921. The main event of the day is from 1752: The cooperation between Sikhs and Mir Mannu snapped as a result of Kaura Mal’s death. Together they span three periods, from Persecution, the Dal Khalsa and Abdali's invasions (1717–1764) to The Gurdwara Reform (Akali) movement (1920–1925). People, places and movements connected with this day include Ahmad Shah Abdali, Mughal rulers and governors, Lahore and Maharaja Ranjit Singh.

Also on this day

  • 1752Diwan Kodha Mal, also known as Mitha Mal, died while fighting in Lahore
  • 1834Peshawar occupied by Sikhs Ranjit Singh sent a force under Hari Singh Nalwa, Ventura and Court under nominal command of Prince Nau Nihal Singh. Pathan chiefs sent their families away as they were aware of the duplicity Of Shah Shujah and Ranjit Singh’s intention to occupy Peshawar. They agreed to enhance the tribute but the Sikh army occupied Peshawar on the pretext that the Prince wanted to see the town and the Pathan chiefs left the city. Hari Singh Nalwa was appointed Governor of Peshawar along with the Governorship Of Hazara. British did not appreciate Sikh occupation of Peshawar. Sikh coins struck from Peshawar.
  • 1921Gurudwara Manak Sahib was forcibly taken over and brought under the control of SGPC

Historical background

Persecution, the Dal Khalsa and Abdali's invasions (1717–1764)

After Banda Singh's death the Mughal governors of Lahore, notably Zakariya Khan and Mir Mannu, put prices on Sikh heads, and many Sikhs, such as Bhai Mani Singh and Bhai Taru Singh, were executed. The Sikhs organised in jathas, united as the Dal Khalsa in 1748 and resisted the repeated invasions of Ahmad Shah Abdali, who killed thousands of Sikhs in the Vadda Ghallughara of 1762 and blew up Sri Harmandir Sahib, which the Sikhs rebuilt.

On this day in this period: 1752 The cooperation between Sikhs and Mir Mannu snapped as a result of Kaura Mal’s death; 1752 Diwan Kodha Mal, also known as Mitha Mal, died while fighting in Lahore.

The Sikh Empire of Maharaja Ranjit Singh (1799–1839)

Ranjit Singh of the Sukerchakia misl took Lahore in 1799, was proclaimed Maharaja in 1801 and united the misls into a single state stretching from Peshawar and Kashmir to the Sutlej. He modernised the Khalsa army, gilded Sri Harmandir Sahib, and kept peace with the British under the Treaty of Amritsar (1809).

On this day in this period: 1834 Peshawar occupied by Sikhs.

The Gurdwara Reform (Akali) movement (1920–1925)

Sikhs organised the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (November 1920) and the Shiromani Akali Dal (December 1920) to free historic gurdwaras from hereditary mahants backed by the government. Through non-violent morchas, including Nankana Sahib (1921), the keys agitation (1921–22), Guru ka Bagh (1922) and Jaito (1923–25), and alongside the militant Babbar Akali movement, the campaign led to the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925.

On this day in this period: 1921 Gurudwara Manak Sahib was forcibly taken over and brought under the control of SGPC.

People and places of this day

Ahmad Shah Abdali

The founder of the Durrani Empire of Afghanistan (c. 1722–1772), who invaded India repeatedly from 1747 to 1767. His campaigns against the Sikhs included the Vadda Ghallughara of February 1762 and the destruction of Sri Harmandir Sahib, but Sikh resistance prevented him from holding Punjab.

Mentioned on 14 other days of the year

Mughal rulers and governors

The Mughal emperors Jahangir and Aurangzeb ordered the executions of Guru Arjan Dev Ji and Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji, and Aurangzeb's successors and the governors of Lahore and Sirhind, among them Wazir Khan, Zakariya Khan and Mir Mannu, led the long campaign against the Sikhs between 1704 and the 1750s.

Mentioned on 26 other days of the year

Lahore

The historic capital of Punjab, where Guru Arjan Dev Ji was martyred (Gurdwara Dera Sahib) and Maharaja Ranjit Singh ruled the Sikh Empire from the Lahore Fort. After 1947 it became part of Pakistan.

Mentioned on 49 other days of the year

Maharaja Ranjit Singh

The founder of the Sikh Empire (1780–1839). He took Lahore in 1799, was proclaimed Maharaja in 1801, unified the misls, built a modern army, and covered Sri Harmandir Sahib in gold, giving it the name Golden Temple.

Read more → · Mentioned on 31 other days of the year

Hari Singh Nalwa

Commander-in-chief of Maharaja Ranjit Singh's army (1791–1837), who extended the Sikh Empire to Kashmir, Peshawar and the Khyber and died defending Jamrud in 1837.

Read more → · Mentioned on 4 other days of the year

The SGPC

The Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, formed at a meeting at the Akal Takht in November 1920 to manage historic gurdwaras, and given legal standing by the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925. It manages Sri Harmandir Sahib and gurdwaras in Punjab, Himachal Pradesh and Chandigarh.
